Rafael, have you seen the news? A website says that your fruit in Rotterdam is bad.
Yes, I saw it an hour ago. It is a rumor for now. Our farms passed every test last month, so it can't be the fruit itself.
But the photos show damaged boxes. What happened?
The temperature log shows twelve degrees, so it must be the container. It might be the cooling unit, but we are still checking.
My client is nervous. This is a crisis for their reputation too.
I understand. We will publish a short statement today, and we will be transparent: what we know, and what we do not know yet.
Good. Who will speak to the press?
I will be the spokesperson. And if it is our mistake, we will apologize and recall the shipment.

Hi Rafael, it is Daniel Visser from Harbor Fresh in Rotterdam. I want to give you the facts before you speak to anyone. We opened container forty-two this morning. About a third of the boxes are damaged, and the fruit is soft. Our technician says the cooling unit stopped for six hours during the trip, so it must be a problem with the container, not with your farms. It might be the shipping company's fault, but we are not sure yet. A journalist called me an hour ago. I told her that we were checking the facts. Please call me before you publish your statement.

I am a journalist, and I write about the food industry. When there is a problem, I call the company. Some companies answer in ten minutes. The spokesperson tells me what they know and promises to call me back with more facts. Those stories are usually short and fair. Other companies say nothing. Then I have to write that the company did not comment, and readers think the worst. My advice is simple: answer the phone. If you do not know the cause, say that it might be one thing or another, and say when you will know more. A rumor needs silence to grow.
Check the facts with the team in Rotterdam. Choose one spokesperson for the company. Publish a short statement on the same day. Answer the questions from the press. Give an update the next morning.
